# Medieval Horizons

by Ian Mortimer

## Why the Middle Ages Matter

## Format:

...

We tend to think about the Middle Ages as a dark, backward and unchanging time characterised by violence, ignorance and superstition. By contrast we believe progress is the consequence of science and technological innovation, and that it was the inventions of recent centuries which created the modern world.  
  
We couldn't be more wrong. As Ian Mortimer shows in this fascinating introduction to the Middle Ages, people's horizons - their knowledge, experience and understanding of the world - expanded dramatically. All aspects of life were utterly transformed between 1000 and 1600, marking the transition from a warrior-led society to that of Shakespeare.

...

It outlines the enormous cultural changes that took place - from literacy to living standards, inequality and even the developing sense of self - thereby correcting misconceptions and presenting the period as a revolutionary era, of fundamental importance in the development of the Western world.

MEDIEVAL HORIZONS

Why the Middle Ages matter  
256pp. Bodley Head. £22.

Ian Mortimer

M _edieval Horizons: Why the Middle Ages_ matter seems to be about the importance of the period of history between late antiquity and the Renaissance — there it is in the title, twice. This is, however, not quite what it delivers. Ian Mortimer posits the book as a response to claims by the historians Yuval Noah Harari and Ian Morris that people’s lives remained fundamentally unchanged over the centuries before the Industrial Revolution. In _Sapiens_ Harari imagines a Spanish peasant falling asleep in the year 1000, waking up in 1500 and feeling right at home.

...

But which centuries? Mortimer has chosen to look at the period between 1000 and 1600. He realizes this end date “might raise questions”, but claims that because there are competing dates for the end of the Middle Ages anyway, there is “no right or wrong”.

...

I agree with Mortimer that “the Middle Ages were not about stasis but hope, vision, effort and change”.

in All , Book reviews , London and UK
Ian Mortimer, Medieval Horizons: Why the Middle Ages Matter , The Bodley Head, 2023.
Reviewed by Charles Freeman
When do the Middle Ages begin and end? I think AD 500 is a good starting point, following the collapse of the Western Roman Empire in 476. Many studies do not get going until 1000 or 1100 and Ian Mortimer, a distinguished medievalist, adopts this approach in his Medieval Horizons. Many scholars, as Mortimer acknowledges, see the 15th century as marking an essential transition, yet he extends his story up to 1600. I shall challenge this at the end of this review.
Traditionally medieval Europe has been described as stagnant and superstitious compared to the chronological bookends of the Graeco-Roman Empire and the Renaissance. Mortimer is an ardent defender of the vitality and diversity of the Middle Ages and this thoughtful book deploys his arguments. An analysis of the historiography of the period adds to the quality of the text. His sources are mainly from England (as have been those of his earlier books).

...

some five miles per hour on horseback. Mortimer does discuss the technological advances of medieval Europe: the amazing complexity of the Gothic cathedrals, the replacing of vellum with paper and the development of the clock. However, if he had included more from mainland Europe he would surely have made his case for the Middle Ages stronger.
